facts.statement: Armadillosuchus lived during the Late Campanian to early Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Campanian-early Maastrichtian~

facts.statement: The genus Armadillosuchus was described by Marinho and Carvalho in 2009.
facts.quote: authority: Marinho & Carvalho 2009

facts.statement: The type species of the genus is Armadillosuchus arrudai, named by Marinho and Carvalho in 2009.
facts.quote: subdivision: A. arrudai Marinho & Carvalho 2009 (type)

facts.statement: Armadillosuchus fossils were found in the Adamantina Formation of the Bauru Basin in Brazil and date to approximately 70 million years ago.
facts.quote: It was described in February 2009 from the late Campanian to early Maastrichtian Adamantina Formation of the Bauru Basin in Brazil, dating to approximately 70 Ma.

facts.statement: Armadillosuchus was a large and robust sphagesaurid crocodylomorph reaching a total length of about 2 meters.
facts.quote: Armadillosuchus was among the larger and more robust sphagesaurids, with a total length of approximately 2 m.

facts.statement: Armadillosuchus possessed heterodont teeth, suggesting it was capable of chewing its food.
facts.quote: Like other sphagesaurids, Armadillosuchus had heterodont teeth and was likely capable of chewing.

facts.statement: Based on its teeth and size, Armadillosuchus is believed to have been an omnivore that ate invertebrates, plants, and possibly scavenged.
facts.quote: Based on its dentition and size, it is believed that it was an omnivore, feeding on invertebrates, plants and possibly scavenging on occasion.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Armadillosuchus's well-developed forelimbs may have allowed it to burrow, potentially helping it regulate its body temperature.
facts.quote: Furthermore, its well developed forelimbs may have made the animal a capable burrower, which could have helped Armadillosuchus regulate its body temperature.

facts.statement: Armadillosuchus is considered one of the best-armored notosuchians due to its distinctive body armor.
facts.quote: The most recognizable feature of Armadillosuchus is its body armor, which makes it one of the best armored notosuchians.

facts.statement: Fossils reveal a rigid shield of hexagonal osteoderms behind the head followed by mobile bands resembling those of armadillos.
facts.quote: Preserved elements show the presence of a rigid shield of hexagonal osteoderms just behind the head, followed by a series of mobile bands similar to those of armadillos that give the animal its name.

facts.statement: Later research suggests that Armadillosuchus's armor may have been deeply embedded in the skin and not fully visible during life.
facts.quote: While this armor is prominent in the fossil specimen, later research suggests that it may not have been visible in life and was instead deeply embedded into the animal's skin.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen UFRJ DG 303-R is a well-preserved partial skeleton including the entire skull, neck, cervical osteoderms, front torso, and a nearly complete left forelimb.
facts.quote: Specimen UFRJ DG 303-R, chosen as the holotype of the taxon, is a well preserved partial skeleton retaining the entire skull, the neck and cervical osteoderms, the front of the torso and a nearly complete left forelimb.

facts.statement: Marinho and Carvalho described a second, less complete paratype specimen consisting of partial upper and lower jaws.
facts.quote: Alongside it Thiago S. Marinho and Ismar S. Carvalho also describe a second, less complete specimen, which they designate as the paratype of Armadillosuchus. This specimen consists of a partial upper and lower jaw.

facts.statement: The genus name Armadillosuchus combines the Spanish word for armadillo with the Greek word for crocodile, referencing the animal's armadillo-like osteoderm shields.
facts.quote: The genus name Armadillosuchus is derived from the Spanish armadillo, chosen due to the superficially similar osteoderm-shields of the two animals.

facts.statement: The species name arrudai honors João Tadeu Arruda for his contributions to the paleontology of the region.
facts.quote: The species name on the other hand was chosen in honor of João Tadeu Arruda for his numerous contributions to the paleontology of the area.

facts.statement: Armadillosuchus had a robust, slightly flattened skull that maintained the oreinirostral form typical of Notosuchians.
facts.quote: The skull is robust and slightly flattened, though maintaining the overall oreinirostral form typical for Notosuchians.

facts.statement: Armadillosuchus teeth included curved caniniforms, protruding incisor-like front teeth, and conical molariform teeth with shearing edges.
facts.quote: These tooth morphologies include curved caniniforms, protruding front teeth that resembled incisors and conical molariform teeth with shearing edges filling the remainder of its mouth.

facts.statement: The ribs of Armadillosuchus show signs of pachyostosis, meaning they were thickened.
facts.quote: The ribs of Armadillosuchus show signs of having undergone pachyostosis, meaning that they are thickened.

facts.statement: Armadillosuchus is a large-bodied sphagesaurid with a skull length of around 300 mm, nearly twice that of smaller family members like Yacarerani and Adamantinasuchus.
facts.quote: Among sphagesaurids, Armadillosuchus is classed among the large-bodied forms with a skull length around 300 mm, nearly twice that of the smaller members of the family (such as Yacarerani and Adamantinasuchus).

facts.statement: In a 2026 review, Kitayama and Bertini provisionally proposed that Armadillosuchus arrudai is a junior synonym of Sphagesaurus huenei.
facts.quote: In a 2026 taxonomic review, Pedro Akira Kitayama and Reinaldo José Bertini proposed that Armadillosuchus arrudai was a junior synonym of Sphagesaurus huenei, together with Caryonosuchus pricei. The authors explicitly regarded this interpretation as provisional.

facts.statement: Kitayama and Bertini argued that the features distinguishing Armadillosuchus arrudai were insufficiently diagnostic and might represent intraspecific variation or deformation.
facts.quote: They considered the characters used to distinguish A. arrudai insufficiently diagnostic, interpreting differences in cranial proportions and ornamentation as compatible with intraspecific variation and preservational deformation.

facts.statement: The proposal to synonymize Armadillosuchus arrudai with Sphagesaurus huenei remains provisional and could change with new specimens or analyses.
facts.quote: Their conclusions were explicitly provisional and could be reassessed using additional well-preserved specimens or quantitative morphological analyses.

facts.statement: Armadillosuchus possessed prominent body armor made of small bony plates called osteoderms.
facts.quote: Like other crocodylomorphs, Armadillosuchus had prominent body armor formed by small bony plates known as osteoderms.

facts.statement: Seven bands of osteoderms formed a mobile thoracic armor that resembled that of modern armadillos.
facts.quote: This is then loosely linked to seven bands of osteoderms that form the mobile thoracic armor, which superficially resembles that of modern armadillos.

facts.statement: The central armor consisted of overlapping rectangular osteoderms decorated with circular pits.
facts.quote: The central portion of this armor is formed by a series of overlapping osteoderms, which are rectangular in shape and ornamented with circular pits similar to those seen in other neosuchians.

facts.statement: Tail osteoderms were generally wider than they were long, ranging from rectangular to subtriangular shapes.
facts.quote: The osteoderms of the tail ranged from being rectangular in shape to being subtriangular, but generally wider than they were long like those of the torso.

facts.statement: The arrangement and morphology of the teeth gave Armadillosuchus powerful, scissor-like jaws.
facts.quote: Both their morphology and the way they are arranged give the animal powerful, scissor-like jaws.

facts.statement: Wear facets on the teeth suggest the animal used a back-and-forth chewing motion similar to Sphagesaurus.
facts.quote: Wear facets seen on the teeth suggests that the animal performed back and forward movement with its jaws in a chewing motion similar to Sphagesaurus.

facts.statement: The robust forelimbs were likely used to dig burrows or forage, possibly aiding in thermoregulation.
facts.quote: The forelimbs in particular may have been used either to create burrows or to dig while foraging, with the former matching with the inferred thermoregulatory behavior of Notosuchians.

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesize Armadillosuchus was an omnivore eating molluscs, arthropods, roots, and pines.
facts.quote: One hypothesis on the dietary preferences of this animal proposes that Armadillosuchus was an omnivore, feeding on a variety of animals and plants including molluscs, arthropods, roots and pines.

facts.statement: It is possible the animal occasionally scavenged dried carcasses, which may have caused the observed tooth wear.
facts.quote: It is also possible that Armadillosuchus scavenged at least occasionally and that the tooth wear seen in the known material was caused by the animal feeding on dried up carcasses.

facts.statement: The animal may have used gastroliths to assist in grinding food alongside its specialized teeth.
facts.quote: Besides the tubercles on the keels of the molariform teeth and the ability to move its jaws back and forth in a grinding motion, Armadillosuchus may have also employed the help of gastroliths to help grind food.

facts.statement: A 2019 study used the OPCR method to analyze the tooth occlusion complexity of Armadillosuchus.
facts.quote: A 2019 study more closely examined the teeth of Armadillosuchus using a method known as orientation patch count rotated (OPCR), originally designed to analyse the complexity of the tooth occlusion in rodents.

facts.statement: Given its large size, an omnivorous diet is considered more likely than an insectivorous one.
facts.quote: While this could be indicative of both insectivorous or omnivorous diet, the latter is more likely given the large size of Armadillosuchus.

facts.statement: The extensive armor has been compared to that of armadillos and ankylosaurid dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The extensive armor of Armadillosuchus has been likened not just to armadillos but also to the osteoderms of ankylosaurids.

facts.statement: It was described in February 2009 from the Upper Cretaceous Bauru Basin in Brazil.
facts.quote: Fue descrito en febrero de 2009 en la cuenca de Bauru en Brasil, del Cretácico Superior.

facts.statement: The genus was named by Marinho and Carvalho in 2009.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Marinho & Carvalho, 2009

facts.statement: The type species is Armadillosuchus arrudai, described by Marinho and Carvalho in 2009.
facts.quote: subdivision: A. arrudai† Marinho & Carvalho, 2009 (especie tipo)

facts.statement: The animal lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Maastrichtian (83.6 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Research indicates Sharpey's fibers ran perpendicular to the outer surface of the osteoderms, unlike in modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: While in modern crocodilians these fibers help keep the bottom of the osteoderms connected to the skin, the study shows that in many Notosuchians including Armadillosuchus, Sharpey's fibers also run perpendicular to their outer surface.

facts.statement: Authors suggest the osteoderms were deeply embedded in the skin and covered by a leathery dermis, similar to modern leatherback and softshell turtles.
facts.quote: A similar condition can be seen in today's leatherback and softshell turtles, leading the authors to suggest that the osteoderms of Armadillosuchus were deeply embedded into the skin of the animal and covered in a leathery dermis.

facts.statement: This deep embedding likely provided the animal with increased flexibility.
facts.quote: This may have had the advantage of increased flexibility.

facts.statement: The osteoderms may have helped absorb and retain heat during basking, allowing high activity levels without direct sunlight.
facts.quote: During basking, the osteoderms may have helped to absorb and retain heat over extended periods of time, helping the animal to maintain high levels of activity even without direct sunlight.

facts.statement: The reconstruction of the armor on the back of the body remains difficult due to only isolated material being known.
facts.quote: However the armor of the back of the body is only known from isolated material and thus difficult to reconstruct.

facts.statement: It is debated whether terrestrial Notosuchians like Armadillosuchus regulated temperature like modern monitor lizards rather than like modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: However, despite this Armadillosuchus and other terrestrial Notosuchians may have regulated their internal temperature in a manner more similar to modern monitor lizards.

facts.statement: The back was covered by armor with flexible bands and rigid protectors similar to an armadillo, reflecting the genus name meaning "armadillo crocodile".
facts.quote: La espalda de Armadillosuchus estaba cubierta por una armadura que poseía bandas flexibles y protectores rígidos similares a las de un armadillo (de ahí el nombre del género que significa "cocodrilo armadillo").

facts.statement: Due to its singular morphology, it is believed to have had a subterranean lifestyle.
facts.quote: Debido a su morfología singular, se cree que tuvieron un estilo de vida subterráneo.

rejected.quote: Each premaxilla only contained two to three teeth, with the second pair being the aforementioned caniniforms that greatly exceed the first pair in size.
